objectives: Describe the independence of French Cameroun on 1 January 1960
Describe the independence of Nigeria in October 1960
Explain the effect on the British Cameroons
reviewNotes: Teacher to verify: dates (1 January 1960; 1 October 1960; the 1959 UN decision) and the wording of the plebiscite options; avoid taking sides in the debate on the options.

Draft for teacher review: only well-established facts are used and the tone is neutral; every date and name must be verified against the official History syllabus and standard references before release.

blocks.md: French Cameroun became independent on **1 January 1960** as the **Republic of Cameroon**, with Yaoundé as capital. This followed years of negotiation, political change within the French system and the work of the UN, which had ended the trusteeship for the French territory. The new state adopted a constitution and elected its first government.

blocks.caption: Years of change
blocks.alt: A timeline from 1958 to 1962 with 1959, 1960 and 1961.

blocks.title: Nigeria
blocks.md: **Nigeria** became independent from Britain on **1 October 1960**. This was important for the British Cameroons because they had been governed as part of Nigeria. The UN now had to decide their future: remaining attached to an independent Nigeria was one possibility, and joining the independent Republic of Cameroon was another.

In **1959** the UN General Assembly decided that a **plebiscite** (a vote of the people) should be held in the British Cameroons to ask them about their future. Both **Southern** and **Northern** Cameroons would vote separately. The question offered two choices: to **join the independent Republic of Nigeria** or to **join the independent Republic of Cameroon**. Some political groups wanted other options, but these were not in the vote.

blocks.title: Be careful
blocks.md:
- Do not say the whole of Cameroon became independent in 1960: only French Cameroun did; the British Cameroons joined later (1961).
- The plebiscite offered two options, joining Nigeria or joining Cameroon; people disagree about this arrangement, and historians discuss it.
- Give dates exactly: 1 January 1960 and 1 October 1960.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Independence of French Cameroun (1 January 1960) is not the same as reunification (1 October 1961).
- Nigeria's independence date (1 October 1960) is a year before reunification, on the same day and month.
- The UN, not Britain or France alone, decided how the British Cameroons would vote.

blocks.title: Example 1: dates
blocks.statement: State the date of French Cameroun's independence and of Nigeria's independence.
steps: Both are in 1960 but nine months apart.

blocks.title: Example 2: the plebiscite choices
blocks.statement: Which two choices were offered to the British Cameroons in the plebiscite?
steps: There were two options on the ballot.
The other was to join the Republic of Cameroon.
blocks.answer: To join Nigeria or to join the Republic of Cameroon.

objectives: Describe the Foumban Conference and the reunification of 1 October 1961
Explain the importance of 11 February and 1 October
reviewNotes: Teacher to verify: dates (11 February 1961; Northern Cameroons joining Nigeria on 1 June 1961; Foumban in July 1961; 1 October 1961), the names of the two states, the origin of national days; vote counts and the debate about the terms of union are intentionally not given.

Draft for teacher review: only well-established facts are used and the tone is neutral; every date and name must be verified against the official History syllabus and standard references before release.

blocks.md: On **11 February 1961** the plebiscites were held. In the **Southern Cameroons** a majority voted to **join the Republic of Cameroon**. In the **Northern Cameroons** a majority voted to **join Nigeria**. The Northern Cameroons became part of Nigeria on **1 June 1961**. For this reason the Southern Cameroons and the Republic of Cameroon were the two units that joined together.

blocks.caption: From plebiscite to reunification
blocks.alt: Four boxes showing the plebiscite, the Northern Cameroons joining Nigeria, the Foumban talks and reunification.

blocks.title: The Foumban Conference
blocks.md: In **July 1961** at **Foumban**, leaders of the Southern Cameroons and the Republic of Cameroon met to discuss the **constitution** for the new union. The discussion led to a **federal constitution** with two federated states, East and West Cameroon, a federal government and a federal president. People still debate the terms of the Foumban talks and later changes.

blocks.title: 1 October 1961
blocks.md: On **1 October 1961** the Southern Cameroons ended British trusteeship and joined the Republic of Cameroon to form the **Federal Republic of Cameroon**. This is called **reunification**, as the two parts of the old German Kamerun were joined again. The Southern Cameroons became **West Cameroon** with Buea as capital; the Republic of Cameroon became **East Cameroon**. Yaoundé was the federal capital.

**Reunification** did not remove all differences: the two parts had different languages, laws, school systems, money and administrative habits. The new state adopted **English and French** as official languages and tried to build a common identity. National days celebrated include **11 February** (Youth Day, from the plebiscites) and **20 May** (National Day, linked to the 1972 referendum), as well as **1 October** in memory of reunification.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- The Northern Cameroons voted to join Nigeria; do not say the entire British Cameroons joined Cameroon.
- Reunification (1 October 1961) is different from independence (1 January 1960).
- The Foumban Conference (July 1961) took place before the union on 1 October.

blocks.title: Example 1: results
blocks.statement: What was the result of the plebiscite in the Southern Cameroons and in the Northern Cameroons?
steps: Southern Cameroons: a majority for joining the Republic of Cameroon.
Northern Cameroons: a majority for joining Nigeria.
Both votes took place on 11 February 1961.
blocks.answer: South: join Cameroon; North: join Nigeria.

blocks.title: Example 2: the new state
blocks.statement: Name the two states of the Federal Republic of Cameroon in 1961.
steps: The Southern Cameroons became West Cameroon.
The Republic of Cameroon became East Cameroon.
Together they formed the Federal Republic.

objectives: Describe the names of the state: Federal Republic, United Republic and Republic of Cameroon
Describe the Constitution of 1996 in outline
reviewNotes: Teacher to verify all dates (20 May 1972; the 1984 renaming; the 1996 Constitution) and the neutral phrasing of the debate about federation; the lesson does not name any person and takes no side.

Draft for teacher review: only well-established facts are used and the tone is neutral; every date and name must be verified against the official History syllabus and standard references before release.

blocks.md: From **1961 to 1972** Cameroon was a **federation** of two states: **East Cameroon** and **West Cameroon**, each with its own government and assembly, under a federal president and federal government. The aim was to protect the identities of the two parts (such as their languages and legal traditions) while building one nation. Federal institutions were in Yaoundé and West Cameroon's in Buea.

blocks.caption: Names and forms of the state
blocks.alt: A timeline from 1959 to 1997 with 1960, 1961, 1972, 1984 and 1996.

blocks.title: The 1972 referendum
blocks.md: On **20 May 1972** a **referendum** was held, in which the people voted on a new constitution creating a **unitary state**: the **United Republic of Cameroon**. The federal structure ended and the two states were merged into one country with one government. Supporters said it would strengthen unity and save costs; others have criticised the loss of federal safeguards. **20 May** became the **National Day**.

In **1984** the country's name was changed to the **Republic of Cameroon**, the name it had in 1960. A new **Constitution** was adopted in **1996** and later amended. It describes Cameroon as a **decentralised unitary state**, with English and French as official languages, and creates **regions**, a **Senate** and other institutions. The decentralisation process aims to give local councils and regions more responsibility.

blocks.title: Changes in the name and form of the state
blocks.md:
- 1960: Republic of Cameroon (French Cameroun).
- 1961: Federal Republic of Cameroon.
- 1972: United Republic of Cameroon.
- 1984: Republic of Cameroon.
The 1996 Constitution is the current basic law, with later amendments.

blocks.title: Be careful
blocks.md:
- This topic is sensitive: present facts and the different views fairly and with respect.
- A federation has two or more states sharing power; a unitary state has one central government with possibly local units.
- Always give dates and names correctly.

blocks.title: Example 1: federation or unitary?
blocks.statement: Which describes Cameroon in 1965 and which in 1975?
steps: In 1965 there were two federated states.
In 1975 there was a unitary state after the 1972 referendum.

blocks.title: Example 2: why 20 May?
blocks.statement: Why is 20 May celebrated as National Day?
steps: It is the date of the 1972 referendum.
The referendum created the unitary United Republic of Cameroon.
So the day celebrates the unitary state.
blocks.answer: It commemorates the 1972 referendum creating the unitary state.
